We were still two days’ tacking from the Company’s new survey camp. I was for carrying on; but the Geologist, looking paler than usual, insisted the afternoon’s crosswind was too unpredictable, that it would be prudent, with the light already beginning to fail, to furl the sails and drop anchor for the night. He added, with a show of technical authority, that if we were to navigate the shifting sandbars ahead, we must do so with the sun high, not low in our eyes. This was logical, I suppose. Twenty miles in this terrain meant a full day’s sailing for our land-yacht, and I could see the dust-devils already spinning like malevolent phantoms at the far end of the basin. Still, I was irritated beyond measure by the halt, and quite unreasonably, I admit, for one more night could hardly signify after so many weeks. As we had a full water-cask, and prudence was apparently our new captain, I brought the yacht to a stop in the centre of the great salt-pan. The pan was a perfect circle, flat and white, with sides that fell away in sharp, crystalline cliffs. The twilight bled into it a bruised purple long before the sun had vanished. A low wind moaned without pause, yet a profound stillness clung to the earth itself. The scattered, petrified trees, their limbs contorted as if in a final agony and glazed with a lacquer of salt, might have been carved from obsidian, to the sharpest splinter, to the most delicate shard. It was not desolation, it was something more; an attitude of waiting. Not a single skittering sound of lizard or insect could be heard. You stared out, astonished, and began to doubt your own hearing, then the night fell like a trapdoor, and you were sightless as well.

Around midnight a sheet of rock far off on the basin’s rim gave way, and the tremendous crash made me start as though a cannon had been fired beside my ear. When the twin moons rose there was a ground-haze, thick and strangely luminous, and more disorienting than the dark. It did not move or swirl; it was simply present, a glowing miasma that hugged the ground like a shroud. At two or three, perhaps, it thinned as a veil thins. We saw for a moment the jagged line of the cliffs, the immense, sterile plain, with the ghostly little discs of the moons floating above it, all utterly silent, and then the glowing veil thickened again, smoothly, as if drawn by an unseen hand. I ordered the winch, which we had begun to crank, to be locked once more. Before the pawl had clicked home, a sound, a very deep and resonant hum, as of immense and patient power, rose slowly from the glowing haze. It stopped. A chorus of rhythmic clicks, arranged in some baffling and alien cadence, reached our ears. The sheer novelty of it made the skin on my neck tighten. I cannot say how it affected the others: to me it was as if the salt-pan itself had found a voice, so suddenly, and seemingly from every direction at once, did this structured and unnerving chorus arise. It culminated in a rapid series of metallic snaps, which ceased abruptly, leaving us frozen in a collection of foolish postures, and straining to hear into the even more unnerving and absolute silence that followed. ‘Saints preserve us, what was that,’ whispered at my side one of the surveyors, a thin, nervous man with spectacles and a new tweed jacket he insisted on wearing. Two others stood dumbstruck for a full half-minute, then scrambled into the main cabin, only to emerge immediately and stand with their surveying poles held like clumsy spears, peering into the gloom. What we could discern was only the yacht we were on, its rigging indistinct as though it were beginning to fray into mist, and a luminous circle of ground, perhaps twenty feet wide, around us, and that was all. The rest of the universe was absent, as far as our senses could tell. Utterly absent. Erased, expunged; swept clean without so much as a whisper or a puff of dust to mark its passing.

I went aft, and ordered the anchor chain to be checked for strain, so as to be ready to slip the mooring and make sail at a moment’s notice if required. ‘Will they come for us?’ a terrified voice asked from the dark. ‘We will be stripped to the bone in this haze,’ another muttered. The faces were drawn with tension, the hands shook, the eyes stared wide without blinking. It was a curious thing to observe the contrast between the expressions of the company men and those of the local guides we had hired, who were as new to this particular salt-pan as we were, though their home village was only a hundred miles to the south. The white men, of course deeply agitated, also wore a singular look of being personally offended by such an outlandish disturbance. The guides had a watchful, naturally absorbed expression; but their faces were fundamentally calm, even those of the one or two who murmured to each other as they tested the tension of the sails. They exchanged a few quiet, clicking phrases, which seemed to put the matter to rest for them. Their leader, a tall, gaunt man of indeterminate age, wrapped in a single piece of dusty red cloth, with sunken cheeks and eyes that seemed to burn with a cold light, stood beside me. ‘Hah!’ I said, merely for the sake of companionship. ‘They sing,’ he stated, with a slight, dry movement of his lips and a glint of worn teeth, ‘they sing. We hear them.’ ‘Hear them, yes,’ I said; ‘but what are they?’ ‘The old ones,’ he replied curtly, and, resting his hand on the tiller, he stared into the haze with a look of dignified and immense concentration. I suppose I would have been properly unnerved, had it not occurred to me that he and his kinsmen must be quite thirsty: that their thirst must have been growing steadily for at least the last three days. They had been contracted for the journey (I do not believe a single one of them had any real conception of a contract, as we at the end of ages of commerce have. They still belonged to the immediacy of things, had no inherited jurisprudence to guide them, as it were), and of course, as long as a chit was signed and filed in some dusty office back at the port, it never entered anyone’s mind to wonder how they might actually drink. To be sure, they had brought with them some dried gourds of brackish water, which could not have lasted more than a day, even if the surveyors hadn’t, in a fit of sanitary panic, emptied a significant number of them over the side. It seemed a summary action; but it was, in their view, a matter of justifiable self-preservation. You cannot be expected to sail with men drinking from what might be contaminated vessels and at the same time maintain your own delicate hold on health. Beyond that, they had been given a weekly allotment of three tin tokens, each stamped with the company’s seal; and the idea was they were to trade these for water at company-approved oases. You can imagine how well that was working. There were either no oases, or the wells were dry, or the Geologist, who like the rest of us drank from sealed canisters, with an occasional bottle of lukewarm wine thrown in, saw no reason to alter our course for some unverified spot on a map. So, unless they planned to suck the tin tokens themselves, or use them to dig for moisture in the salt, I fail to see what benefit their handsome wages could be to them. I will say it was dispensed with a punctuality befitting a grand and enterprising colonial venture. For the rest, the only thing to eat I saw in their possession was a bag of dried, leathery fungus, of a pale grey colour, they kept in a leather pouch, and would occasionally break off a piece of, but so small it seemed more a ritual gesture than any true act of sustenance. Why in the name of all the parched devils of thirst they did not simply overpower us, they were ten to four, and seize the water-casks for themselves, is a thing that astonishes me now as I consider it. They were sinewy, tireless men, with little capacity for weighing long-term consequences, with endurance, with a quiet desperation, even now, though their lips were cracked and their eyes had sunk deeper into their skulls. And I saw that some principle of restraint, one of those human mysteries that defies all logic, was at work in them. I looked at them with a sudden sharpening of focus, not because it occurred to me that I might be murdered for a cup of water before morning, though I confess to you that at that moment I saw, in a new light, as it were, how fleshy and full of liquid the surveyors appeared, and I hoped, yes, I genuinely hoped, that my own aspect was not so, what is the word, so, un-drained: a touch of ghoulish vanity that seemed of a piece with the hallucinatory quality that had infected all my days in that place. Perhaps I had a touch of the sun, as well. One cannot keep a thermometer forever pressed to one’s own brow. I often had ‘a touch of the sun,’ or a touch of other things, the siren song of the salt, the preliminary whispers before the louder madness that would inevitably follow. Yes; I watched them as one watches men who hold a secret one is not meant to know, but which one’s life may shortly depend upon.

beings who were not in the least human. Not in the way I understood it, at any rate. One felt a kinship with a dog, a horse, even with the sly, independent spirit of a cat; but these men, with their dark, unreadable faces and their profound, silent economy of movement, seemed to belong to another order of creation altogether. They were a part of this landscape of heat and death, and we, with our fussy anxieties and our canteens of precious, sloshing life, were the trespassers, the unnatural apparitions. The silence that followed my thought was of a piece with it, a vast, hollow thing that pressed in from the shimmering horizon. The heat was no longer merely an affliction of the skin; it was a state of being, a viscous medium through which one had to push, breath by breath. The sun, a malevolent white disk, had burned all the blue from the sky, leaving a bleached, fibrous canopy overhead. It was a sky made of cataracts.

Then a new thing began. It was not a sound, not at first; it was a vibration, a low thrumming that you felt in the soles of your boots, in the very marrow of your bones. It seemed to rise from the baked salt of the pan itself, a deep, resonant hum like a single, impossibly vast string being plucked in the earth’s core. I saw one of the surveyors, the one with the perpetually startled expression, put a hand to his ear as if to clear it of water. The fat man with the binoculars, who had been scanning the horizon for some imagined relief, lowered his glasses with a clatter against his chest. His mouth hung open, a dark circle in his sun-blasted face. ‘What is that?’ he whispered, and the question was absurd, a child’s query in the face of a geological pronouncement. The sound grew, not in volume so much as in presence. It was in the air now, a low, mournful drone that seemed to have no source and therefore came from everywhere. It was the song of the salt, the anthem of desolation.

The Geologist, who had been staring at his charts as if they were holy scripture, looked up slowly. His face, usually a study in composed, academic authority, was slack with a kind of intellectual bewilderment. He was a man of rock strata and fossil records; a humming desert was outside his field of expertise, an anomaly that defied his ordered world. ‘Atmospheric pressure,’ he announced, to no one in particular. ‘An inversion of thermal layers, most likely. Creates an acoustic phenomenon.’ He said it with the air of a man reassuring himself, but his eyes darted about, trying to catch the phenomenon in the act of being merely scientific. It was no good. The sound was not scientific; it was religious, a liturgical chant for a god of emptiness. It filled the mind, leaving no room for explanations.

I glanced over at the guides. They had not moved. They stood or squatted in a loose group, their stillness a rebuke to our own twitching agitation. Their faces betrayed nothing, but they were listening, I knew. They were not hearing a noise; they were receiving a message. Their headman, a man whose age was impossible to guess, with a face like a dried riverbed, was slowly tracing a spiral in the salt with his bare toe. The hum seemed to coalesce around him, as if he were its focal point. I found myself walking towards him, my boots crunching with obscene loudness on the crystalline ground. The sound seemed to part for me as I moved, then close in behind me. The Geologist called out something, a warning perhaps, but his voice was thin, a gnat’s whine lost in the immense, resonant drone.

I stopped a few feet from the headman. He did not look up. He continued his slow, deliberate drawing. The spiral grew, ring by patient ring. I had the absurd notion that if he completed it, something would happen, that the world would either end or begin anew. ‘What is this sound?’ I asked. My own voice sounded strange to me, a foreign intrusion.

He finished a loop of his spiral before he answered. He did not raise his head. His voice, when it came, was like the rustle of dry leaves, yet I heard it perfectly, a kernel of clarity in the universal hum. ‘The land sings for the thirsty,’ he said. He paused, and then added, ‘It is an old song. It calls them home.’ He looked up then, and his eyes were not empty; they were full of a vast, weary knowledge, the knowledge of a man who had heard this song many times before. He looked past me, at the surveyors who were huddled together near the water-casks, their faces pale and slick with sweat. ‘The land is patient. It will have its drink.’

I stepped back as though I had touched a live wire. The simple profundity of it, the terrible, dispassionate logic, was more chilling than any threat. It was not malice I saw in his eyes; it was a statement of natural law, as inescapable as the sun above us. We were not enemies to be fought; we were merely vessels of the water the land craved. The humming was its call, a siren song for the liquid in our veins. I walked back to my place by the land-ship’s tiller, and the world seemed altered, clarified. The Geologist’s scientific pronouncements, the surveyors’ terrified whispers, our whole elaborate pretence of being on a mission of discovery, it all seemed a kind of shrill, meaningless gibberish in the face of that one, simple truth. The land was thirsty.

As the sun began its long, slow descent, the humming faded, sinking back into the earth, leaving behind a silence that was somehow more menacing than the noise had been. The sky to the west became a wound. It bled out in colours for which there are no names, lurid purples and feverish oranges, streaks of septic green and veins of raw, bloody crimson. It was not a beautiful sunset; it was a morbid spectacle, the gaudy decomposition of the day. We watched it, mesmerised, as if it were a public execution. In the dying light, the salt pan turned a soft, deliquescent pink, the colour of exposed flesh. Mirages, which had tormented us all day with their promises of water, now writhed on the horizon like dying spirits, their forms stretching and dissolving in the violent light.

The Geologist called the four of us white men together. ‘We cannot stay here,’ he said, his voice low and strained. ‘That… phenomenon, may return. It is unsettling for the men.’ He meant it was unsettling for him. ‘The map indicates a potential cistern in a rock formation twelve miles to the northeast. An old trade route marker. If we start at first light, we can make it before the worst of the heat.’

‘And if the cistern is dry?’ asked the fat surveyor, his voice trembling. ‘Or if it is not there?’

The Geologist fixed him with a look of cold fury. ‘It is our best option. The alternative is to remain here until our water is gone and we…’ He did not finish the sentence. He did not need to. We had all heard the land’s song. ‘We will post a watch. Two hours each. I will take the first.’

The night came on not as a gentle fading, but as if a black cloth had been thrown over the sky. The stars that appeared were not the familiar, friendly lights of a European sky; they were sharp, cold, and remote, chips of ice in an infinite void. The air grew cold with a shocking rapidity. We, who had been praying for relief from the heat, now shivered, our sweat turning to a clammy chill on our skin. The contrast was a physical blow, another of this land’s casual cruelties. I took my watch, the second, after the Geologist’s. The silence was absolute. The land-ship, our ungainly mechanical camel, loomed like the skeleton of some prehistoric beast. The surveyors were huddled in their bedrolls, whimpering in their sleep. The guides, however, were awake.

They had built no fire. They sat in a circle a short distance away, wrapped in their thin cloths, motionless as the stones that littered parts of the pan. They were not speaking. They were not sleeping. They were simply sitting, their faces turned up to the indifferent stars. I felt a pull, a curiosity that was stronger than my fear. I walked over to them, my steps noiseless on the salt. The headman seemed to sense my approach without turning his head. He made a small gesture with his hand, an invitation to sit. I sank down on the cold, hard ground, feeling the chill seep into me. For a long time, we all just sat there, staring at the sky.

Then, the headman spoke, his voice a low murmur that did not seem to disturb the silence. ‘You have a water-devil in your man,’ he said.

I was confused. ‘A what?’

‘The fat one. With the glass eyes. He wastes his soul looking for what is not there. Soon, his soul will be so thin, the devil will drink the rest of him.’

He was talking about the surveyor with the binoculars. I thought of his constant, frantic scanning of the horizon, his desperate belief in a salvation that lay just beyond sight. A water-devil. It was a perfect description. It was a sickness of the spirit, this relentless, hopeless looking. ‘He is afraid,’ I said, lamely.

‘We are all afraid,’ the headman corrected me gently. ‘Fear is the first drink the land takes. But his fear is a hole without a bottom. He tries to fill it by looking out. He should be looking in.’ He tapped his own chest with a long, bony finger. ‘The water is here. The quiet is here. If you have the quiet inside, the land’s song is only a song. If you have noise inside, it will call you apart.’

We sat in silence again. The stars wheeled overhead, their slow progress the only movement in the whole universe, it seemed. I thought of his words. This was the secret, then. This was the restraint I had witnessed. It was not a moral code, not in my sense of it. It was not a fear of consequences or a respect for our authority, which they must have known was a fragile sham. It was an internal discipline, a deep, abiding quietness that made them immune to the panicky thirst that was hollowing us out from the inside. They were not waiting for us to die so they could have our water. They were simply enduring, in the same way the rocks endured, with a patience born of an understanding I could only dimly grasp. They knew that the land would take what it was owed, and they had made their peace with it. We, on the other hand, were fighting it, bargaining with it, trying to outwit it with our maps and our instruments, and in doing so we were only making ourselves more tempting, more succulent, to its insatiable thirst.

The fat surveyor let out a thin, terrified scream in his sleep. One of the guides next to me made a soft, tutting sound, a sound one might make at the antics of a foolish child. The headman looked at me, and for the first time, I thought I saw a flicker of something like pity in his eyes. ‘You should have a care for your own quiet,’ he said. ‘You listen too much. To him. To the ground. To your own thoughts.’

He was right. I was an observer, a collector of impressions and sensations. My mind was a noisy, cluttered place, full of the echoes of other men’s fears and the hum of the earth. I had no quiet of my own. I was just as vulnerable as the fat man with his binoculars, perhaps more so, because I was aware of the disease. I saw then, in the cold, crystalline starlight of that salt pan, that this journey was not about reaching a destination. It was about what would be stripped away from you before you got there. It was a process of reduction, of being boiled down to your essential truth. For the surveyors, that truth was a gibbering, hollow fear. For the Geologist, it was a faith in a science that was utterly powerless. For the guides, it was a stony, unbreachable peace. And for me? I did not know. I was afraid to find out.

When my watch was over, I did not sleep. I lay in my bedroll, my eyes wide open, and listened to the beating of my own heart, a frantic, liquid drumming against the great, dry silence of the world. And I hoped, yes, I positively hoped, that the land was not listening too closely.

But the presence, the weight of a thousand hostile eyes, was gone. We had not defeated them. We had, it seemed, simply offended their ears.

The manager was staring at me with a look of awe and terror, as if I myself were some kind of dangerous lunatic. And perhaps I was. And his subjects, the unseen people in the woods, had fought for him. This was not a man who wanted to be saved. This was a man who had to be captured. The journey up the river had ended. The hunt had just begun.

He was seeing the darkness that had been his companion, his inspiration, and his undoing. The darkness that was not a place, but a condition. His whole life, his triumphs, his degradation, his soaring ambitions and his vile acts, all of it had culminated in this one moment of supreme knowledge.

‘And what are those?’ I asked, my voice flat.

‘To get the ivory,’ he said simply. ‘That is all. To get the ivory, and to stay alive. Everything else is… talk. Just talk.’ He gestured vaguely at the dark jungle. ‘He was good at the talk. ‘No,’ the manager said, and he leaned closer, his breath sour with cheap spirits. ‘The first rule is not to listen to the jungle. It whispers to you. It tells you things. It tells you that there are no rules. That you can do anything you want. Kurtz listened. That was his mistake. You, captain… you look like a man who has been listening too.’

He straightened up, his moment of drunken confidence passing. He looked at me one last time, with his cold, calculating eyes, and then he turned and walked away, disappearing into the shadows of the main cabin.
